essays.title: if (document.layers): the web forks in two
essays.description: In 1997 Netscape and Microsoft each invented their own model of a web page. Everyone wrote every effect twice, and the way it ended explains a lot about how the web still works.
unverified: That the "Best viewed with" buttons were usually 88 by 31 pixels. The buttons are well documented; I did not open a source for the size.
The mention of Dynamic Drive as a source of copy-and-paste scripts. Its site would not load when this was checked.
Why the two browsers exposed such different models. The engine explanation is my best guess, and the essay says so.

essays.title: Where did all the old web developers go?
essays.description: Around 2008 nobody writing JavaScript seemed to be over 40, and the industry spent a decade arguing about why. The answer was arithmetic, and the same arithmetic is running again.
unverified: Vivek Wadhwa's 2010 TechCrunch piece and the original 2009 "Plan B" essay are named from secondary references. I did not open either directly.
The Stanford and ADP employment figures are quoted from SoftwareSeni's summary, not from the study itself.
The CNBC figure on senior job postings is quoted from Fullstack's summary of CNBC's reporting.
That the staff and principal engineering track spread through the 2010s is my reading, not a sourced claim.

essays.title: getYear() and the year 19100
essays.description: One small Date method returned 100, 2000 or 100 again for the year 2000 depending on the browser, got fixed three different ways, and is still in every browser today.
unverified: The January 2000 sightings of "19100" (the US Naval Observatory, Meteo-France, the Gore campaign site) rest on Wikipedia's Year 2000 problem article, not on the original news reports.
Internet Explorer 9's return to "year minus 1900" in standards mode rests on one reference page.
JDK 1.1 is dated only to February 1997, because sources disagree on the day.
Whether Navigator 4.0 to 4.05 returned 100 or 2000 could not be pinned down, so the essay speaks only about 4.06 and later.
Why Navigator 3 changed the method is my guess, and is marked as one.

essays.title: jQuery 1.0: what $ really replaced
essays.description: jQuery 1.0 shipped in August 2006 with a dollar sign borrowed from another library, and replaced a folder of copy-pasted fixes that its own author had been winning contests with.
unverified: When the "write less, do more" slogan first appeared. It is sourced only to Wikipedia's citation of the jquery.com page title.
The date of the first release. The jQuery project says January 14, 2006; John Resig's own write-up implies the 15th. The essay reports both.
Whether the jquery-1.0.js file on the jQuery CDN is identical to the one released on August 26, 2006. Its header carries an October 2006 revision date.
Why jQuery 1.3.2 used querySelectorAll only for document-rooted queries is my inference.
John Resig's age at the time comes from Wikipedia.

essays.title: View Source was the school
essays.description: For about fifteen years the web trained its own workforce through one menu item that showed how any page was made, and then the pages stopped being readable.
unverified: Netscape's exact menu labels and keyboard shortcut for viewing source. The essay says only that the name varied by browser and year.
Tim O'Reilly's essay is linked in its print view, because the canonical page refused to load.
That the Firefox bug reporter copied the script from a page's source is an inference, and is worded as one.
Why Internet Explorer opened source in Notepad rests on a single 2008 Microsoft blog post.

essays.title: Firebug: the first look inside the page
essays.description: In January 2006 one developer uploaded a few days of code as a Firefox add-on, and within a few years every browser had copied its panels, its F12 key and its console.log.
unverified: Joe Hewitt's own 2006 blog posts. His site is down, so his words are quoted only as they appear in Mozilla Hacks and a FOSDEM interview.
The January 12, 2006 announcement date comes from Jay Hoffmann's history of the web, and is flagged in the text.
That F12 as the developer-tools key began with Firebug 0.2.3 rests on Wikipedia, and is attributed to it.
The Firebug 1.1 source listings come from a third-party mirror, which the essay names.

essays.title: XMLHttpRequest: six years waiting for a name
essays.description: Microsoft shipped the object behind every web application in 1999, under a name its author calls an excuse. Almost nobody used it until a designer's 2005 essay called the technique Ajax.
unverified: Almost everything about how XMLHTTP was written and shipped rests on one account, Alex Hopmann's. He gives no date for the weekend, the naming or the security review beyond starting the webmail work "probably sometime in late 1998", and his page shows no original publication date.
Jesse James Garrett's essay is linked as a saved copy of its print view, because Adaptive Path's own site would not load.

The dates for Mozilla, Safari 1.2 and Opera 8.0 support come from Wikipedia, as do Oddpost's 2002 opening and the release months of Internet Explorer 5 and 7. Wikipedia's XMLHttpRequest article also dates the idea to 2000, which contradicts Hopmann; I followed Hopmann.
Jay Hoffmann's history of the web says XMLHTTP was added to replace Java components that Outlook Web Access had relied on. Hopmann does not mention this, so I left it out.

How little the object was used before 2004 is hard to measure. Aaron Swartz wrote that nobody he knew used it, but Hopmann says the approach was already doing well by 2000 to 2002, and it was common on corporate intranets.
Google's two blog posts are linked for their dates only. Whether Google Maps used XMLHttpRequest or hidden frames at launch is disputed in the comments on Swartz's post, so the essay does not say.

That XMLHTTP sitting behind ActiveX held back public sites, that Prototype's wrapper kept most developers from typing the constructor, and that the missing name mattered as much as I say, are my own readings.

essays.title: The webmaster: a mailbox that became a job
essays.description: "Webmaster" was coined as a mail alias on a style page, grew into the title for whoever ran the whole site, and faded, while the address in the footer link outlived the job.
unverified: That "webmaster" was coined on the etiquette page rests on Tim Berners-Lee's own note on that page. The 1993 date is my inference from a November 1992 snapshot without the word and Merriam-Webster's first-use year.
That the W3C folder named MailArchive/webmaster holds mail sent to the webmaster address is my reading of its name and of the greeting in one message. The archive itself does not say.
The 1996 Web Week survey is quoted from an undated Princeton Review career profile. I could not find the survey itself, and Georgia Tech's webmaster surveys from the same years would not load.
Louise Addis as the first webmaster, and the reasons the role faded, rest on one secondary source, Jay Hoffmann's history.
Google's 2008 "Webmaster Team" and webmaster job ladder rest on one person's blog post.
Microsoft's advisory on the live.fi certificate does not name the mailbox that was registered, so the essay does not either.
That address harvesting drove webmasters to scripts and forms is supported only by Wikipedia and by RFC 2142's warning. The FTC's 2002 study of harvesting would not load, so it is not cited.
The four forces behind the one-person job, and the comparison of the server administrator with an on-call rotation, are my own readings.

essays.title: The IE6 funeral: campaigning to kill a browser
essays.description: In March 2010 a Denver web shop buried Internet Explorer 6 in a pine coffin and Microsoft sent flowers. The browser had a fifth of the market that night, and what finally ended it was not persuasion.
unverified: The card's exact wording. I quote TechCrunch's version; Computerworld printed it slightly differently ("See you at MIX where we'll show..."). Attendance also varies, from "around a hundred" to "between 80 and 100".

I did not open ie6funeral.com or the original 37signals, Digg, IE6 No More and Windows blog posts (those I tried would not load), so the obituary, the 37signals notice, the Digg figures and Roger Capriotti's words are quoted from press coverage and other blogs that reproduced them.
The Digg poll result. Eric Lawrence's post adds two answers to get 69% who could not upgrade, while TechCrunch reported 77%. The poll was self-selected either way.
Everything about the YouTube banner's origin and effect rests on Chris Zacharias's own account, written ten years later, including the claim that YouTube's IE6 audience halved in a month.
The "Retiring IE6" post is signed only "Eric". I name Eric Lawrence because it is on the IEInternals blog; the page itself does not give a surname.

That the YouTube banner mostly moved home users, that IE6 Countdown's launch a year to the day after the funeral was a coincidence, and the remark about most browsers now running on Google's engine are my own inferences. I also did not open a source for Chrome's 2008 launch.

essays.title: JSConf 2009: the community that didn't know it existed
essays.description: In April 2009 about 130 people met in a hotel outside Washington for a conference about JavaScript itself. It nearly didn't happen, and its format, its side room and its name spread around the world.
unverified: Whether this was strictly the first JavaScript conference. The organizers and attendees called it that, Kevin Dangoor hedged with "possibly", and I did not search for earlier events in other countries.

The story of the mortgage-backed deposit, the drive to the hotel and the emails rests on Jan Lehnardt's 2015 speaker notes alone. Dangoor's 2010 notes confirm only that the conference was nearly cancelled and that a "sold out" notice produced a waiting list.

Who proposed taking JSConf to Europe, and when Chris Williams first raised the idea. Lehnardt and Williams each remember making the offer, and Lehnardt's 2009 post says Williams asked "last fall" while the 2015 talk places it just after RubyFringe.
The attendance figure. Dangoor wrote 130, Lehnardt "130+ attendees & speakers", and the sponsor pitch promised 125. I found no official count.
That the Ajaxian blog's founders organized The Ajax Experience. I only opened the event archive, which lists Ben Galbraith as a speaker, so the essay says no more than that.

How many editions JSConf EU held, whether JSConf US ran in every year after 2015, and who owns the JSConf name now. The sites I opened give a "10th anniversary" in 2019, a 2019 event in Carlsbad and a 2025 event "under the OpenJS Foundation", and nothing firmer.
That scarcity made community conferences harder to get into, that no library had been "the host" before, and that the job title needed the room. Those are my readings, not sourced claims.

essays.title: The blogs and the feed reader: an industry run by correspondence
essays.description: From about 2004 to 2013, front-end development argued, reviewed and patched itself across a few personal websites, and Google Reader delivered the whole exchange until Google switched it off.
unverified: Ajaxian itself. The site no longer serves its archive and I could not reach an Internet Archive copy, so its story rests on Dion Almaer's announcement, other people's mentions and an index of its titles. That its founders joined Mozilla in 2008 comes from one of those titles, not from the entry.

The inside story of Google Reader (the Fusion prototype, the 30 million peak, maintenance mode, the pope) comes from one article in The Verge, and its source for the 2013 announcement had already left Google.

The early RSS dates, the Bloglines sale, the adoption of the feed icon and GitHub's launch month come from Wikipedia. The RSS 2.0 specification's own history says August 2002 where Wikipedia says September, so I wrote only the year.
Feedly's 500,000 new users is the company's own figure, as relayed by The Next Web.

Peter-Paul Koch's 2004 article on inline event handlers is known to me only through Simon Willison's quotation of it, and Apple pointing to QuirksMode for JavaScript documentation is Koch's own account.
That links moved to Twitter, Reddit and Hacker News, that code moved from blog entries to GitHub, and the comparison of a patched blog entry to a pull request are my own readings.

essays.title: JSLint and The Good Parts: the subset that became the language
essays.description: Douglas Crockford's linter and thin book told developers which parts of JavaScript to stop using, which started a fork and a fight over a semicolon and left much of its advice inside the language.
unverified: I could not open the book itself or O'Reilly's page for it, so the publication month, the back cover text and the page numbers come from Crockford's own site and an Open Library record, and the one passage I quote from chapter 1 comes from Wikiquote.

Sources disagree on when JSLint first appeared: the Wirfs-Brock and Eich history cites its web page as 2001, while the JSHint project's history and the copyright line say 2002, and I have not seen a dated release.

The older JSLint documentation I quote is an undated copy on a university course site, and Crockford's 2001 essay is quoted from the page as it stands now, which has been revised since, so I can't say which year any particular wording dates from.

Anton Kovalyov's 2011 post is quoted from a copy in a Disqus repository because the original address no longer loads, and its quotations of Douglas Crockford and Brendan Eich are Kovalyov's attributions, which I could not trace to their origins.

That strict mode is JSLint's subset moved into the language is my own argument: the Wirfs-Brock and Eich history traces it to Crockford's recommendations to the committee and does not mention the tool. That ESLint's rule names descend from JSLint's option names, and that a frozen standard is why the subset caught on, are also my readings.

essays.title: YSlow: the letter grade that made front-end performance a job
essays.description: How a Yahoo research chart, thirteen rules and a Firebug add-on that graded pages from A to F turned page speed from a server problem into a front-end discipline.
unverified: I could not open the Internet Archive from where I was working, so I never saw the 2007 versions of Yahoo's YSlow page, its rules page or the Yahoo Developer Network release announcement; the rule text and Apache lines I quote come from the rules page as it stands now, which has been edited since.

I read the YUI Blog research articles in an archived copy hosted at derek.io, not on the original site. That copy bylines Part 1 to Tenni Theurer and Part 2 to "YUI Team"; a September 2007 YUI Blog post calls Theurer the author of the whole series.

I did not open Yahoo's own release announcement. The July 25, 2007 date comes from posts stamped that day and may be July 24 Pacific time, the OSCON link rests on two bloggers that week, and the early scores and rule weights from Simone Chiaretta are quoted from Jeff Atwood's post, not from Chiaretta's own pages.

The grading code I show is from the later open-source release, not the 2007 extension. That the E grade was added after 2007 is my inference from scores in the fifties being reported as F that summer.

I found no statement of when YSlow was last released or how long the Firefox add-on kept working; that its Firefox version ended with Firebug in 2017 is my inference, and so is the claim that these rules did more than any framework to make a build step normal.

essays.title: Cornify: unicorns on every page
essays.description: How a 2009 joke about single-feature startups put glittery unicorns on ESPN and Stack Overflow with one script tag, a bookmarklet and a Konami-code snippet.
unverified: I could not open the Internet Archive's 2009 captures of cornify.com or its script, so my account of the original code rests on the copy committed to GitHub in April 2011 and on what people described in 2009.

The history of the wrappers around the script is thin: I found Paul Irish's snippet, John Hobbs's Unicorn Blitz and a 2010 Hacker News thread, but no official jQuery plugin and no count of how many sites used any of them.

I found no report naming who put the unicorns on ESPN.com or confirming whose Konami code was used; that they sat there for weeks rests on one line in Paul Irish's post, The Register later dated the prank to April Fools' Day, and my suggestion that ESPN's wrapper called the script several times is a guess from how the reports describe it.

I name Christoph Ono only from the GitHub profile of the account that maintains the repository, which links to the studio in Cornify's footer; the Cornify site and its Hacker News account never give a person's name.

The claim that Cornify began as a spoof of single-feature startups comes from the user-written Know Your Meme entry, Stack Overflow's 2009 joke is known to me only from the company's 2010 blog post, and my guess that the url parameter fed the home-page counter is an inference from the code.

essays.title: Annex B: the features the web kept
essays.description: The JavaScript standard keeps escape(), substr, "text".blink() and HTML comments in an appendix of things it would delete if it could, and that appendix went from optional advice in 1999 to a requirement for every browser.
unverified: I read Netscape's early JavaScript reference in a mirrored copy on a university server, because the Internet Archive would not open for me. The mirror carries no date, and I placed it in the Navigator 3 era from its "Implemented in Navigator 3.0" entries.

The "icky" classification of __proto__ and the remark that the committee agreed to move syntax items into the main body come from comments on two GitHub pull requests, which I read through an automated page summary and not line by line.

That the unescape(encodeURIComponent()) trick became a familiar way to feed btoa(), that it helps keep escape() from being removed, and that it accounts for a fair share of today's escape() calls are my own impressions. I have one 2006 blog post for the trick and no usage figures.

The third edition gives no reason for moving escape() to the annex. Tying it to the function's handling of Unicode is my reading, and the "C++" search-box example is my illustration, not a documented incident.
The history paper says substr was "moved" to Annex B in 1999. I found no mention of it in the first or second edition, so I say the annex was its way into the standard.

essays.title: Wat: the jokes about [] + {}
essays.description: Gary Bernhardt's four-minute talk "Wat" and the wtfjs site turned JavaScript's type conversions into a running joke, and every punchline, from [] + {} to a line that only works because {} is parsed as a block, is the specification doing what it says.
unverified: I did not watch the video of "Wat": I quote it from the caption file on its own page, which has transcription slips, and I take what appeared on screen, the jsc console and the exact " Batman!" line from the Stack Overflow question and Hacker News comments written that week.
I date the talk to January 2012 from the conference's name and from write-ups and Hacker News submissions dated January 18 to 28; I found no page giving the day it was delivered.

That wtfjs began in February 2010 rests on the dates of its oldest posts and its own about page; I never saw the original Tumblr site, "about 120 posts" and "dozens of contributors" are my counts from the repository, and that Brian LeRoux spoke on PhoneGap at the first JSConf rests on the JSConf essay in this collection, not on a source I opened for this one.

Stack Overflow and GitHub refused my direct requests, so I read the question and answer through the Stack Exchange API and the repositories as clones; the vote and point counts are what those services reported on the day I looked.

Three claims are my own inference: that the missing try statement helps explain why + returns a string, that making Symbol and BigInt throw was the committee's answer to the coercion jokes, and that JSFuck's practical use is evading filters. I did not open the Sla.ckers.org discussion JSFuck credits, and I found no first author for the banana joke beyond what Denys Dovhan's list says.

essays.title: #!: the URLs no server ever saw
essays.description: From 2010 Twitter and then Gawker put their pages behind twitter.com/#!/name addresses that only JavaScript could read, and the outage and argument that followed sent rendering back to the server.
unverified: Twitter's 2012 engineering post "Improving performance on twitter.com" would not load for me, at its current address or in the Internet Archive copy the essay links. Its text, date and byline come from NBC News, .net magazine and The Next Web, and I could not check them against the original.
The five-hour length of the Gawker outage rests on Mike Davies's essay alone. Other writers confirm the outage, but none gives a duration, and I found no account from Gawker of what failed.

Dan Webb's tweet about undoing Twitter's hashbang URLs is known to me only through Ubergizmo's report. Webb's essay "It's About The Hashbangs" is gone from Webb's site, so I rely on other pages for its existence and title.
Ben Ward's "Hash, Bang, Wallop" would not load either. The line of Ward's I quote is an earlier remark, taken from Davies's essay and not from its original page.

I could not open Google's full crawling specification, which now redirects to a general page, so the mechanism is described from the 2009 proposal and the 2017 notice. That Twitter's seeded request cache is an ancestor of today's hydration data, and that the scheme worked as permission for new hashbang sites, are my own readings.

essays.title: The Rhino book: when the bookstore was the curriculum
essays.description: From 1996 a book with a Javan rhinoceros on the cover was how you learned JavaScript, and the shelf it sat on explains why web books were thick, yearly and sometimes sold in beta, and where their reference pages went.
unverified: O'Reilly's own pages for the old editions would not load for me, so I read the 1997 and 2002 editions' prefaces, acknowledgments, colophon and copyright page in an unauthorised web copy of O'Reilly's CD Bookshelf, which I have not linked. I could not compare that text with a printed copy, and I never saw the 1996 beta edition itself.

Sources disagree about which Navigator 3.0 beta the beta edition covered. The 1996 book list says the 3.0b4 release, while the second edition's preface says the final beta and its acknowledgments mention Beta 6 features.

Flanagan's 2011 post about pirated copies is gone from his site, and I know its words only from Mark Bernstein's quotation, which does not give the post's own date. Nothing I read connects that post to Flanagan joining Mozilla the same year.

Mike Hendrickson's statement that the computer book market halved between 2000 and 2004 comes from an O'Reilly post I could not open, quoted on a librarian's blog. The same quotation admits O'Reilly had reliable sales data only from 2004, so the size of the fall is the company's estimate.

That the books were thick because thick books sold is Philip Greenspun's account of what publishers believed, not publisher data. A founder's recollection, hedged with "I believe", is my only source for Computer Literacy's stores closing in 2001.

The animals I give for the HTML, Webmaster, Dynamic HTML and CSS books come from the colophons of editions published from 2000 to 2002, and I did not check the 1990s covers. That the 1997 CD-ROM belongs to the line O'Reilly later called the CD Bookshelf, that reviewers at both Netscape and Microsoft show the book filled a gap in vendor documentation, and that the unauthorised copies now work as an archive are my own readings.

essays.title: The tracker that got JavaScript an off switch
essays.description: In February 1996 a commuter's demo page showed that Netscape 2.0 let any site watch where you browsed next, and three weeks of public argument with the language's author ended in a patch, a $1,000 prize and the first preference to turn JavaScript off.
unverified: The tracker's own source code is lost: it was served by a program on an OSF machine that no longer answers, so my account of how it worked comes from LoVerso's descriptions, and the statement that the 2.01 patch stopped one window reading another site's address is my reconstruction from them.

No source says the preference to disable JavaScript was added because of LoVerso's report. He asked for a button, an unnamed correspondent asked Eich for the same thing, and there was other pressure at the time, so "the report that did most to get JavaScript an off switch" is my reading.

The Thursday-night bounty call comes only from Keith Dawson's newsletter, which places it after the RISKS post, while the RISKS header is dated Friday morning; I followed the header. The Naval Research Laboratory advisory also rests on Dawson alone, and I could not find any of the 1996 press articles themselves, so the Mercury News front page and everything else I say about the coverage rest on LoVerso's own list of it.

I know Brendan Eich's message of February 29, 1996 only from Alex Kremer's repost to a mailing list the next day, and I could not open Netscape's own 2.01 release notes or security note, so Netscape's side rests on that repost, Frank Hecker's unofficial note, the CIAC bulletin and TidBITS.

Sources disagree on when Navigator 2.0 shipped: TBTF of February 10, 1996 says it was released the week before and LoVerso was testing it on February 13, while "JavaScript: The First 20 Years" gives March 1996. I followed the 1996 sources.

That the idea became working code in one evening is my inference from the timestamp on the sample log entry, and reading the same origin policy's later wording as a description of the Tennyson, Weston and LoVerso bugs is my own interpretation.
I know Eich's 2012 talk only from its abstract, as kept by a conference index, and have not seen the talk or its slides.

essays.title: left-pad: the eleven lines npm had to un-unpublish
essays.description: Azer Koçulu lost the package name kik to a messaging company, asked npm how to delete everything he had published and was sent the command; when he ran it on March 22, 2016, one of his 273 packages was left-pad, and two and a half hours later npm broke its own rule to put it back.
unverified: I could not open either Medium post: Azer Koçulu's "I've Just Liberated My Modules" or Mike Roberts's "A discussion about the breaking of the Internet", which holds the emails. Every line I quote from them comes by way of Ars Technica, The Register, The Verge or people quoting them on Hacker News that week, and neither post is linked.

That npm sent Koçulu the command that deleted his packages rests on Koçulu's own account: he told Ars Technica in 2016 that it came from Isaac Schlueter, and his 2024 essay says only that npm provided a script. npm's post-mortem doesn't mention it, and I have not seen the email. The March 18 date for npm's decision comes only from Wikipedia's summary of the emails, and I don't know what day Koçulu asked to leave.
Sources disagree on how many packages were removed: npm's post-mortem and The Verge say 273, The Register said more than 250 that night, and Koçulu's 2024 essay says there were more than 350.

I read the GitHub issue through a text rendering of the page, so the 2:27 PM unpublish by Koçulu and the 2:47 PM unpublish by Westland's account come from registry records pasted there, not from the registry itself. That the 2:47 unpublish and the 0.0.9 release were a second attempt at a usable version number, that 0.0.3 shares 0.0.9's timestamp because of how npm restored it, and that left-pad's downloads fell because of Babel's fix are my inferences.

That Kik never published anything under the name kik is what the registry's version list shows now; a release that was published and later removed would not appear there, and I found no statement from Kik or npm about why a placeholder went up the day after the name was transferred.
I could not find the date on which left-pad was marked deprecated; the registry shows the notice on every version but not when it was added.

essays.title: X-UA-Compatible: the default that lasted 42 days
essays.description: In January 2008 Microsoft, with help from web standards advocates, proposed that IE8 should render like IE7 unless a page opted in with a meta tag; the standards world turned on itself, Microsoft reversed the default 42 days later, and the tag's discouraged value, IE=edge, ended up in the templates anyway.
unverified: I could not open Microsoft's press release of March 3, 2008. The sentence given to Brad Smith and the 899 million euro fine come from InformationWeek's report, and the February 21 date for the Interoperability Principles rests on a comment Eric Meyer left under the "Meta-change" entry, as does the remark that the IE7 default was never the IE team's first choice.

Sources disagree by a day or two on the dates. Wilson's post and its comments are dated January 21, 2008 and say the A List Apart article went up that day, while the magazine's own page dates it January 22; my count of forty-two days runs from Wilson's post. The February pair of articles is dated the 19th by Zeldman and Meyer and the 21st by the magazine's page. I have the date of the IE team's post about Beta 2 but not the release date of Beta 2 itself.

I could not find Jeremy Keith's first response, a January 2008 entry called "Broken", so the argument is taken from Keith's A List Apart article a month later. The reply about pages burned onto CDs is anonymous in the archived copy of Wilson's post, and I don't know who wrote it.

No source I opened says why Microsoft changed its mind beyond the reasons in Hachamovitch's post. That complaints might have cost IE's engineers their jobs is Zeldman's speculation, and that the legal sentence is what made the reversal winnable is my guess. Spolsky's account of the beta is one person's browsing, and I found no figures for how many sites broke.

The check-in comment "With great reluctance, admit X-UA-Compatible exists" is unsigned in the bug record, and the link from the bug to the spec change returned an error, so what the validator accepts comes from Michael[tm] Smith's comment there and I have not read the spec text itself. The March 21, 2011 date for HTML5 Boilerplate 1.0 comes from the project's later changelog, and I am assuming the v1.0 file I read is that release. That Sam Ruby wrote the Apache lines is my reading of Dubost's page, and its seventeen links are counted as the page stands now.

essays.title: IMG: the tag that shipped mid-argument
essays.description: In February 1993 Marc Andreessen proposed an image tag that already worked in Mosaic; Tim Berners-Lee and others answered with more general designs, Mosaic 0.10 shipped IMG seventeen days later, and the losing ideas came back as ALT, ISMAP and the wording of the standard.
unverified: Every time and interval in the 1993 thread is worked out from the Date headers of the messages, which come from different machines and time zones; Tony Johnson's is marked PDT in February, and the archive files Andreessen's proposal under February 26 because it converts to UTC. Treat "a little over two hours" and "just under eight hours" as approximate.

I could not open the demo page Andreessen announced with Mosaic 0.10 (the host is gone and the Internet Archive holds only a 404), so what the first IMG release did comes from its release notes alone. I have not run Mosaic 0.10, Midas or Viola: that Midas 2.0 had an ICON tag and Viola had bitmap tags rests on one sentence each from their authors.

That the "Lou" who suggested ALT to frans van hoesel was Lou Montulli of Lynx is my inference from Montulli's June message and Dougherty's report that Lynx supported the attribute; the message says only "Lou". Likewise "Dan C" as Dan Connolly is an inference from van Rossum naming Connolly in the same thread.

That the 1992 tag list had no image element rests on one preserved copy that I searched. Raggett's HTML+ paper carries no date I could find, and I did not confirm the publication date of HTML 4.01, so the essay gives neither; that HTML 4.01 made ALT required is read from the element definition on the one page of it I opened.

Several judgments are mine and not any source's: that holding HTML steady for the RFC track, with no amendment procedure I could find in the thread, left a browser release as the only way to add a feature; that RFC 1866's wording is Berners-Lee's EMBED and PRESENT model; that OBJECT lost to IMG for pictures in practice; and that srcset is a relative of the format negotiation Raggett wanted. I also did not check when srcset entered the standard.

That Raggett both proposed the end-tag idea and wrote a spec that entrenched IMG rests on the author line of HTML 3.2 and on the HTML+ paper; the HTML 4.01 page I read names no author, so I do not credit OBJECT to anyone. The "single-hop principle" is Andreessen's phrase, and "a page had been one fetch" is my gloss on it.

essays.title: Cookies: the standard said off, the browsers said on
essays.description: In 1997 the cookie's own standard said third-party cookies should be off by default. Lou Montulli, who invented the cookie at Netscape and co-wrote that standard, was the one who left them on, and his reasoning was still winning in 2025.
unverified: That Montulli personally made the decision to keep third-party cookies on rests on his own 2013 account, which gives no date beyond "around 1996". Kristol's paper does not say who decided.

Sources disagree on the origin. Montulli says the cookie began with a shopping server built inside Netscape, and Kristol says a customer asked for it. Kristol dates the first Navigator with cookies to September 1994, Montulli says the autumn, and Mozilla's page says version 1.0.

I could not open the Financial Times article of 12 February 1996. Its date and its role come from Kesan and Shah's 2004 study, and nothing I read connects it to the standards group's wording of the same month.

Dwight Merriman's "99%" message, Koen Holtman's browser test, the count of 69 messages and the 2001 study of rejected cookies are all taken from Kristol's paper. I did not open the original list messages or the study.

That Safari was the first mainstream browser to block all third-party cookies by default is WebKit's own claim. Safari had blocked some of them for years before 2020, and I did not trace that earlier history.

That third-party cookies are still on by default in ordinary Chrome windows is my reading of Google's 2025 announcements, which say only that Chrome keeps its "current approach". The comparison between Chrome's 2020 argument and Montulli's is mine, and so is the link from RFC 6265's warning to Pathfinder.

essays.title: FormMail: the contact form that mailed anyone
essays.description: Matt Wright wrote FormMail in high school in 1995 and it became the web's default contact form; it took its recipient from the page, spammers turned it into a mail relay, and the author ended up offering the London Perl Mongers' replacement from the same download site.
unverified: I never saw FormMail 1.6, the version that was abused, or versions 1.7 and 1.8. The code I quote is from the 2009 release, and I rely on the 2002 Bugtraq advisory for what earlier versions did. The advisory says nothing checked the recipient before version 1.9, while the Readme's history says 1.7 and 1.8 added and fixed such a check, and I could not settle which is right.

Sources disagree about when FormMail began. The Readme's history says June 11, 1995, the script's header says June 9, and the Bugtraq advisory says July 9. That it was downloaded two million times is Wright's own figure and I found no second source for it.

I could not open SecurityFocus, so the ranking of FormMail attacks as third in its top attacks for early 2002 comes from the nms news page, and I did not read the earlier advisories the Bugtraq authors cite. The May 2002 date for Wright's redesign and nms page also comes only from the nms site; the copy of Wright's page I read is from 2009.

The Readme credits an advisory at a PDF address on Guilmette's site that would not open for me. I assume it is the same text as the Bugtraq posting I read, which points to a PostScript copy at the same path. The Bugtraq archive masks e-mail addresses, so I have put the @ signs back into the exploit strings I quote, and the JavaScript demonstration is something I know only from the advisory's mention of it.

The 2017 comment under Dave Cross's article is hard to parse. It does not say whether the scripts were Wright's FormMail or the reader's own work built on it, or how the mail was being sent, so I can't say the old recipient or referer holes were the cause.

I found nothing from Wright about the weeks in 2002 when the advisory's authors could not reach the author, so the essay has only their side of that. That the script spread because people who could not program could use it is my inference from the Readme's list of uses, that Cross was one of the London Perl Mongers is my inference from the article's use of "we", that spammers came to FormMail because open relays were being blocked is one administrator's theory from 2001, and that the script's convenience and its flaw were the same design decision is my own reading.

essays.title: YUI: the toolkit Yahoo gave away, and the notice that ended it
essays.description: In 2006 Yahoo gave away the toolkit its own pages ran on, with a CSS reset, a grid, a browser policy and a lecture series attached. In 2014 it stopped, and the engineer who signed the notice wrote the next day that the announcement should have come sooner, maybe a year sooner.
unverified: How long YUI had been winding down before the announcement rests on one sentence in Julien Lecomte's reply on the mailing list, hedged with "Maybe a year ago" and speaking of new development, not releases. Releases went on until 3.18.1, and I have no source for who at Yahoo made the decision, or when.

The thread from Isaac Schlueter to npm is my own connection. The résumé, the YUI Compressor changelog and the Increment interview each say what I report, but none of them ties npm to YUI, the words "at Yahoo" in the interview are the interviewer's bracket, and it does not say which package manager Schlueter used there.

The Dom.get comment and my description of Reset come from the final YUI 2 build in the yui/yui2 repository, not from the 2006 files, which I could not open. I also could not open Yahoo's original Graded Browser Support article, so I describe the policy from the blog's August 2006 update, and the documentation I link is the copy at clarle.github.io, not Yahoo's own site.

Sources disagree by a day about the launch: the welcome post is dated 12 February 2006, while the library announcement and Yahoo's 2014 notice say 13 February. The dates for the YUI 3 beta and the 2014 releases, and the talks by Schlueter and John Resig, are post titles in the archive's index, and I did not open those posts. The Ext JS dates come from Jay Garcia's 2017 history, the 3.18.1 date from Wikipedia, and the post counts from the archive itself.

Several readings are mine: that SimpleYUI was an answer to jQuery, that Zakas's local alias is what Crockford meant, that the blog was a larger gift than the library, and that the rewrite cost YUI its momentum. How widely the end was expected before the notice I can't say; Liferay and some posters point to earlier hints, including a July blog comment I know only from a poster's quotation. I list the FLOSS Weekly episode as further listening without having heard it.

essays.title: The pop-up ad: a separate window for good intentions
essays.description: Around 1997 Ethan Zuckerman moved an ad into its own window at Tripod to keep a car company off a user's page; the trick spread when ad prices collapsed, a Mozilla bug report about porn sites worked out the rule that tamed it, Microsoft adopted the same rule in 2004, and ten years later the apology arrived as an aside.
unverified: I could not open The Atlantic's own pages for Zuckerman's essay or for Adrienne LaFrance's short item about the first pop-up. The passage I quote is as First Things, Gizmodo and Entrepreneur reproduced it, word for word alike, and none of those copies shows brackets, so that the apology was a parenthetical comment is Zuckerman's own description a month later, as are the 300 words and the forty news outlets. The "original sin" line is as NBC News quoted it, and his remark to Wired is taken from Engadget because I did not open Wired.

Sources disagree about the essay's date within August 2014. The History of the Web cites August 8, while Wikipedia's citation and the earliest coverage I read say August 14, so the essay says only "August 2014".

I found no copy of Tripod's original JavaScript or Perl, so the code I show is from Netscape's 1999 documentation and not from Zuckerman's script. The date of late 1996 or early 1997 is from his own biography page, which carries a 2013 date and has been edited since, and NBC's "1997" is the only other date I found.

I could not establish which browser blocked pop-ups first, and I found no source for Internet Explorer's share of the market in these years. That Opera had a setting by July 1999 is what one Mozilla bug reporter says they had read, Wikipedia's claim that Opera was first carries a citation-needed tag, and I found no Opera release note. That Internet Explorer had nothing built in before Service Pack 2 rests on InternetNews in 2003 and on Wikipedia. I also did not confirm which Mozilla release first carried the preference (the bug's approval says 0.9.4 and its milestone field says 0.9.5) or the date Service Pack 2 finally shipped.

Bugzilla shows the commenter who proposed the user-action rule and the person who marked the first bug "Future" only by e-mail address, so I have not named them. Bug dates and intervals are worked out from Bugzilla's UTC timestamps, so a local date may differ by a day. For the two 1999 requests, the Outlook Web Access bug and the New York Times bug I read only the opening comments, and that "invalid" meant Mozilla judged the Outlook problem to be the site's is my reading of the bug's status and its Tech Evangelism category.

On Microsoft's archived copy of jeffdav's post every comment is labelled Anonymous, and the author appears only as jeffdav. That the reply about checking for null is jeffdav's is my inference from its wording, and I describe the chat-client developer from a single comment. That the first Service Pack 2 release had the blocker off is my reading of InternetNews's phrase "a complete about face".

The ad prices are one Adweek editor's estimate in a Fox News piece whose year I take from its contents, and the description of the present-day pop-under rests on Wikipedia alone. That the nsnull line is why a blocked call returned null in Mozilla is my reading of the code. The connections I draw between the porn-site bug and the car company, between Microsoft's rule and the Mozilla comment, and between the 2001 argument over the word "privacy" and Zuckerman's essay are my own.

essays.title: The 1998 CSS wish list: item 28 and the fifteen-year wait
essays.description: In December 1998 the CSS working group published a numbered list of 67 features people kept asking for; the list's own editor wanted item 28, symbolic constants, left to outside tools and said so at length in 2008, and it shipped in 2014 as custom properties, a design neither side had proposed.
unverified: The count of what shipped is my own rough tally and not a W3C figure. The 28 items rest on the specifications' publication histories and on MDN's browser compatibility data, which is a secondary source; the 21 I believe never arrived have no source behind them, and 11 I did not check. Matching later features to 1998 items (the typed attr() to item 45, View Transitions to item 18, clamp() to the 1997 syntax) is my reading.

That Firefox 31 was the first release with custom properties rests on MDN's compatibility data; Firefox's own notes for that release record only the prefix changing to --, and for Chrome I read a beta announcement and not a stable release note. Microsoft's page says filters and transitions came with Internet Explorer 4.0 and above, and I did not establish which release first had the Page-Enter tag or whether it was out before the Note.

The Note is dated 10 December 1998, but Bos's announcement of 24 December says it was published "last weekend", and I could not tell which is the day it went public. I found no published results of the feedback form, and I could not open the working group's newer, members-only list, so I do not know what it added.

Sass's changelog carries no dates and I could not open a dated record of the first LESS release, so the essay does not say when either tool gained variables, only that Sass was popular by February 2011. That the August 2012 meeting was in San Diego on the 14th comes from Glazman's and Atkins's own write-ups and not from the minutes, and I found no source for how the grammar objection to the double dash was settled.

Several connections are my interpretation: that Bos's reply of 31 December 1998, which is about macros, already holds the reasons Bos gave against plain constants in 2008; that Bos was defending an author who works in a graphical editor; that Hyatt's withdrawal, for which I have only the reason Hyatt gave, was the refusal that counted; and that inheritance put the feature beyond a preprocessor. That Bos said nothing about custom properties rests on a search of mailing-list subject lines, and the line on Bos's home page calling constants a bad idea has no date.
